\hlchaptermodality{26}

\section[\ar{ليل}]{\ar{ليل} (layl) — \textquotedblleft{}night,\textquotedblright{} yawm's partner across the whole Semitic family}

\label{lesson:AR-C26-layl}



\begin{quote}
You've already met \emph{layl} once, tucked inside \emph{muntaṣaf al-layl} (\textquotedblleft{}midnight\textquotedblright{}). Now it gets the same standalone treatment \emph{yawm} just did — and the same pan-Semitic family story.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{ليل} — \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\ar{ليل}} (\textbf{layl}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{night}\textquotedblright{} — is the word already hiding inside \textbf{muntaṣaf al-layl} (\textquotedblleft{}midnight,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 15, literally \textquotedblleft{}the half of the night\textquotedblright{}). Root \textbf{l-y-l}.

\begin{culture}
Just like \emph{yawm}, \textbf{layl} is a genuine \textbf{Common Semitic} word, not an Arabic-only term with distant relatives. It traces to \textbf{Proto-Semitic} \emph{\textbf{*layl-}}, cognate with Hebrew \textbf{\he{לילה}} (\emph{layla}/\emph{laylah} — the same word in the famous Passover question, \textquotedblleft{}\emph{mah nishtana ha-layla ha-zeh},\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}why is \textbf{this night} different\textquotedblright{}), Aramaic/Syriac \textbf{lēlyā}, and Akkadian \textbf{līliātum}. Day and night, \emph{yawm} and \emph{layl}, are \textbf{both} words the whole Semitic family has shared for millennia.
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
Be honest about one genuine scholarly debate: linguists don't fully agree on whether Proto-Semitic had this simple \textbf{triradical} \emph{*layl-} form, or a \textbf{reduplicated} \emph{*laylay-} form instead (the doubled shape possibly surviving in some daughter languages' declension patterns). This is a real, open question in comparative Semitics — not settled the way the basic Hebrew/Aramaic/Akkadian cognate set is.
\end{culture}
